look_here_first: SILVER BLUESTEM — LOOK HERE FIRST: find a narrow, silver-white cottony flowering head made of MANY short, crowded hairy rames along a central axis, then examine several actual culm NODES. Nodes are usually pale and glabrous or only short-hairy, NOT cane bluestem's dramatic long white beard. Compare KR bluestem's few long terminal fingers. For a verified identification, examine a true ~2 mm membranous ligule and one attached SESSILE fertile + PEDICELLED sterile spikelet pair with a 1-mm scale; the fertile lemma, not a glume, bears the single bent/twisted awn. Do not use 'no rhizomes' as an absolute key: published Texas sources disagree on short basal rhizomes.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Clumping warm-season grass with smooth pale nodes and a contracted, densely silvery-white fuzzy panicle composed of many short rames; awned sessile spikelets are embedded among conspicuous hairs.

project_inclusion.range_basis: 24-county boundary audit 2026-10-14: Uvalde qualify; Val Verde, Kinney out-of-zone and excluded from PASS. Previous evidence preserved in range_audit; third approved county pending.

morphology_keys.habit: Warm-season perennial, usually tufted/bunch-forming with sometimes semi-prostrate lower culms. ROOT BASE SOURCE CONFLICT: Texas A&M's legacy subsp. torreyana account describes no rhizomes; the UT Williamson County specimen treatment explicitly describes short horizontal rhizomes (to ~4 mm diameter) and basal adventitious roots. Do not certify or reject silver bluestem from rhizome presence/absence alone; document the actual connected crown.
morphology_keys.nodes: Nodes are generally smooth/glabrous and pale to whitish.
morphology_keys.leaves: Many leaves are basal; blades are flat, rough on the upper surface and margins.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Contracted narrow panicle containing many short rames; dense pale hairs make the flowering/fruiting head look silver-white and cottony.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Paired spikelets occur on the rames; sessile spikelets are awned, with long surrounding hairs contributing to the silver appearance.
best_field_traits: Perennial bunchgrass, often with semiprostrate lower culms and pale, generally glabrous stem nodes.
Terminal white-silvery cottony narrow panicle, often up to 20 cm long.
Numerous (>10) very short dense fuzzy rames/branches, each much shorter than the main panicle axis.
Leaves often basal, with rough blade surface and margins.
Distinguish from fanlike cane bluestem with a heavily bearded node, and from KR's several long narrow exposed fingers.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Silver bluestem: narrow contracted oblong densely silvery head with many short rames and typically pale, glabrous nodes. Cane bluestem: wider fanlike many-branched panicle and a thick hair beard at true nodes. KR bluestem: several longer, slender fingerlike racemes clustered at the tip; node hairiness varies and is not proof. Bushy bluestem: broad brushy crown built of paired spathe-subtended rames; inspect inflorescence architecture rather than white color alone.

ecological_notes.habitat: Dry prairies, limestone and rocky sites, roadsides, and open grasslands in Central, South, and West Texas.
ecological_notes.learning_note: Texas literature often still uses Bothriochloa laguroides subsp. torreyana; the learner retains that synonym so field guides and nursery/restoration references remain understandable.

taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Bothriochloa torreyana. Older Texas sources commonly call the same native concept Bothriochloa laguroides subsp. torreyana or var. torreyana. Current Kew also accepts B. laguroides sensu stricto as a separate Mexico-to-South-America species, not a Texas native concept; the stale project B. laguroides row is therefore merged into B. torreyana rather than counted separately.

crew_sequence: Capture complete flowering head and its entire upper stem; its very numerous short hairy rames form a narrow cottony plume.
Trace branching within the head: silver's short crowded branches are unlike KR's long fingers and cane's broad fan.
Examine 2–3 true stem nodes for pale, usually smooth tissue; absence of long nodal beard supports silver against cane but should not decide species alone.
Photograph a leaf collar and mature attached spikelet pair with an actual ruler, ideally 1-mm markings.
Where neither a complete head nor node can be examined, label silver/KR/cane bluestem candidate rather than assigning species confidently.

locally_useful_distinctions.cue: Several LONG thin fingerlike racemes in a terminal cluster; stiff papilla-based hairs on upper leaf blade near collar support ID
MANY SHORT silky racemes occur separately on branching upper leafy stems; often a tight clump
Usually 2–6 relatively STOUT exposed racemes near one terminal point, often turkey-foot
Dense broad BRUSH of crowded short silky paired racemes, subtended by spathe-like leafy sheaths
Dense long soft hair BEARD at stem nodes plus broad FAN of many silvery branches
Single narrow-to-open golden BRANCHED PANICLE and conspicuous pointed membranous 'rifle-sight' ligule
Relatively narrow silky inflorescence of paired rames partly held in long flattened spathe-like sheaths

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.source_concept: Measurements below from A. C. Gibson's UT Williamson County treatment of Bothriochloa laguroides subsp. torreyana, mapped to the existing accepted Bothriochloa torreyana card; Texas A&M's broader legacy account differs in rhizomes and head size. Neither treatment's dimensions are measurements from installed photographs.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.look_here_first: NARROW COTTONY MANY-SHORT-RAME head + pale usually smooth or short-hairy TRUE stem nodes; then check attached sessile/pedicelled pair, lower glume and fertile lemma awn. A hairy silver plume alone is not a species identification.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.growth_and_collar: Perennial usually 35–120 cm, clumped/semi-prostrate lower culms. UT Williamson: short horizontal rhizomes may occur, whereas Texas A&M reports no rhizomes; document rather than force a binary. Nodes glabrous to pilose with hairs up to about 2 mm in UT treatment; contrast cane's conspicuous long nodal beard. True ligule generally membranous about 2–2.4 mm in UT treatment, variably ciliate; distinguish the free membrane from adjacent collar and sheath hairs. No auricles in that treatment.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.head_and_rames: Narrow silvery contracted panicle of numerous short ascending hairy rames; UT Williamson specimen: initial head ~35–70 mm long with 6–10 primary branches, whereas Texas A&M's broad field account allows heads up to 20 cm and >10 branches. Count actual rames on one attached panicle; don't equate a single photographed short rame with the entire inflorescence.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.attached_pair: Each fertile sessile spikelet is paired with a smaller sterile PEDICELLED spikelet on a hairy ~1.5–2.5 mm pedicel. UT Williamson: sessile spikelet mostly 3.8–4.5 mm; pedicelled sterile partner ~2.2–3 mm. Photograph both partners, the hairy rachis internode and pedicel as connected structures; hairs up to ~6–9 mm on internodes are NOT awns.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.glumes_and_florets: Sessile fertile spikelet: lower glume flattened/inrolled, typically 7-veined, short appressed hairs below midpoint, without a secretory pit; upper glume folded, about 2.3–3 mm, usually 3-veined and glabrous. Lower sterile floret has a separate slender ~3 mm lemma and a very short palea (<1.5 mm); upper fertile floret has a narrow ~1.7–2 mm lemma, its single vein continuing into the awn. Pedicelled sterile spikelet generally has two glumes (lower ~7-veined, upper ~3-veined) and lacks normal lemmas/paleas.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.lemma_awn: ONE awn belongs to the narrow UPPER FERTILE LEMMA of the SESSILE spikelet, not the lower glume or the hairy rachis. UT Williamson reports ~8–12.5(–16) mm, red/twisted below and bent around one-third from base; can age straw-colored. The lower sterile lemma is distinct and not the source of that awn.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.central_texas_lookalikes: B. barbinodis (cane): conspicuous long soft beard on true culm nodes and broader fanlike silvery head; B. ischaemum (introduced KR): a few comparatively LONG terminal fingerlike racemes and different collar/spikelet details; Schizachyrium scoparium: many separated short racemes distributed along branching upper leafy stems; Anatherum glomeratum: dense brushy flowering units associated with upper spathes. White hairs, plant height, and smooth-looking nodes alone are not conclusive.
NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: Same documented Texas specimen: rooted crown, intact upper culm and complete narrow many-short-rame head, with centimeter scale; record rhizome state rather than assuming absent.
True blade–sheath junction opened flat with 1-mm ruler resolving the ~2 mm membranous ligule, any marginal cilia, and adjacent sheath hairs separately.
A true pale culm node and attached short hairs with millimeter scale; matched cane-bluestem long-bearded node photographed at the same scale.
At 10–20×, one ATTACHED sessile fertile + pedicelled sterile spikelet pair, measured 3.8–4.5 mm vs ~2.2–3 mm, showing the actual hairy rachis internode and pedicel.
At 20–40×, detached lower/upper glumes, lower sterile lemma and upper fertile lemma with 1-mm ruler, actual 7/3-vein counts and the fertile lemma's 8–16 mm bent awn insertion.
Matched same-scale Texas silver/cane/KR flowering-head views with source-vouchered species and per-photo public display rights.
NEEDS_SITE_QA: Keep all three original physically archived copyright/unknown-license images excluded from PUBLIC rendering; source/creator/license metadata must remain unchanged.

Confirm both Matt Lavin CC BY-SA 2.0 JPEGs are physically present and displayed with creator, source, license and appropriate SA attribution; one is a mixed-community habitat view, NOT an isolated silver specimen.
Check the two existing gross head arrows against original pixels; no microscopic ligule, glume, lemma, awn insertion or nodal beard arrow is authorized until that organ is actually resolved.
Verify live species-page rendering and image-rights preflight separately; a canonical JSON commit is NOT proof of Pages publication.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.public_ready_criteria: Practical crew recognition can remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS, but do not label FINISHED until locally/species-vetted measured ligule, attached spikelet pair, glumes, fertile lemma awn and matched look-alikes are photographed with rights and arrow/site QA. Preserve unresolved project county-native status, original taxonomy concept and all original image records.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SHORT RAMES IN A SILVERY HEAD
field_id_short_tiles.short: Many short crowded hairy flowering branches form a narrow cottony plume
field_id_short_tiles.details: Start with Matt Lavin's genuine silvery panicle (panel 0), then see Austin flowering habitat (panel 7). Trace the MANY SHORT crowded hairy flowering branches along a central axis, not just their white hairs. Compare introduced KR (panel 4): several longer finger-like terminal racemes. A detached fuzzy head alone is insufficient.
field_id_short_tiles.status: AUTHENTIC LICENSED SEEDHEAD PHOTOGRAPHED; whole crown-to-head sequence missing

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED CROWN AND RHIZOME CAUTION
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial bunchgrass; some sources document short rhizomes
field_id_short_tiles.details: Finally, physical CC0 Denver Botanic Gardens and Smithsonian source-vouchered silver herbarium photographs show actual EXPOSED ROOTS attached to BASAL SHOOT CROWNS, unlike the earlier Arizona standing clump with its roots hidden. The complete real specimens are from Colorado and New Mexico respectively; do NOT claim verified Hays County live rhizomes or stolons from preserved-root pictures. Trace upper flowering shoots down through the shared shoot base into attached roots. Native silver is typically bunch-forming; short rhizome reports vary among regional floras.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ROOTED PHOTO ROLE NOW COVERED: two CC0 cataloged true plant-root sheets plus original Arizona flowering clump; local living rhizome form still unresolved

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · LOOK AT THE TRUE CULM NODES AND LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually pale, smooth-to-short-haired nodes; a genuine ~2 mm membrane
field_id_short_tiles.details: See new actual Texas panels 17, 18, 19 in order: opened INNER leaf collar with pale unmeasured transverse rim; separate dark purple-brown TRUE culm node; OUTER leaf-sheath junction. Compare prior photographed true nodes (11–12) and Denton blade–sheath junction (9). Do not teach a measured ligule, constant node color or hairlessness where no calibrated scale is pictured.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL SPECIES-VERIFIED TEXAS OPENED COLLAR AND CULM NODES — millimeter scale still missing

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · SEE THE SPIKELET PAIR, NOT JUST FLUFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile fertile unit alongside a smaller pedicelled sterile unit
field_id_short_tiles.details: Liz Makings' Arizona macro (panel 5) resolves an elongated spikelet, bent/twisted awn and long pale hairs. NEW independently licensed, research-grade 2026 Deer Park Texas close-up (panel 9) also shows several oblong golden spikelet bodies with long silk on a genuine flowering segment. Two arrows identify visible bodies and hair ONLY; neither picture proves exact sessile fertile/pedicelled sterile attachments or upper fertile lemma awn insertion. Bob Harms BOLAT-s and BOLAT-9 remain original copyrighted external scientific references; don't invent mm-scale organ labels.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PARTIAL 0.5/1 — Arizona spikelet and Texas flowering segment both visibly photographed; connected paired organs and 1mm scale still missing

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · DISTINGUISH THE BENT AWN FROM SILKY HAIRS
field_id_short_tiles.short: The upper fertile lemma bears one longer bent/twisted awn
field_id_short_tiles.details: See the actual BENT AWN on Liz Makings' physically archived Arizona panel 5 and compare to the pale flexible surrounding hairs. Its point of origin from the upper fertile lemma of a sessile spikelet is a published botanical claim, not anatomically traced to a visible insertion in the present 720×540 image. Bob Harms' copyrighted BOLAT-9 macro (panel 3) supplies additional external context. We need a dissected linked specimen with mm scale before labeling any particular lemma or glume.
field_id_short_tiles.status: AWN AND SILK visibly documented with arrows; measured fertile-lemma insertion NOT photographed

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLICATION GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Silver vs cane vs KR: node hairs, rame lengths, and a measured pair
field_id_short_tiles.details: Seven documented noncommercial site-permitted silver bluestem photographs now live in the GitHub species images directory: two New Mexico Matt Lavin CC BY-SA, one Arizona Liz Makings spikelet, one Arizona Max Licher connected flowering clump, one Austin smallcurio CC BY, and NEW 2026 Texas CC BY-NC leaf–sheath junction from Denton and hairy flowering group from Deer Park. Three historical images remain rights/ID held and excluded. Two copyright-retained Bob Harms originals remain external educational references, and three Dan Tenaglia Kansas microscopic comparison sources LINK ONLY. Silver's numerous short silky rames contrast with introduced KR's relatively fewer, longer terminal fingers; verify multiple characters before any removal. NEW TWO TEX Herbarium real rooted flowering plants with attached fibrous roots and clear CC BY 4.0 image permissions add the previously missing basal/root anatomy; these are pressed specimens (Guadalupe/Gaines County), not field-grown comparison photographs. No claim of absent rhizomes or photographed free ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 9 public-usable physically archived species photos; real Texas node photographed, measured true ligule, exposed roots and linked mm spikelet pair outstanding

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Silver bluestem photo-first crew identification
steps: 1 · FOLLOW THE SILVERY HEAD: numerous SHORT crowded hairy rames cluster along a narrow axis, unlike the relatively FEWER LONG terminal KR fingers.

2 · CONFIRM A REAL CONNECTED CROWN: new Denver Botanic Gardens and Smithsonian preserved-silver specimen photographs show attached actual basal roots, unlike an undug roadside clump. Compare the Arizona living flowering bunch. This does not settle whether a local Texas stand has any short rhizomes.

3 · SEPARATE SPIKELETS FROM THEIR HAIRS AND AWNS: the original Arizona macro shows the elongated spikelet body, long bent awn and fine surrounding hair. NEW TEXAS panel 10 shows a genuine attached hairy flowering segment, but its fertile sessile/pedicelled member attachments are not sufficiently exposed to label individually.

4 · OPEN A COLLAR, THEN FIND A DIFFERENT STEM NODE: new Milam County panels 17 and 19 show INNER versus OUTER blade–sheath junction; panel 18 shows a distinct, truly transverse CULM NODE on the stem. Earlier Texas panels 11–12 are other actual node views. These new images have NO calibrated millimeter ruler and do not prove ligule length or universal node hairlessness.

5 · RULE OUT NATIVE/INTRODUCED LOOK-ALIKES: KR has longer terminal racemes; cane has a long nodal beard; little bluestem's many shorter racemes are separately subtended by upper leafy shoots. Leave uncertain native plants standing.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Actual CC BY Texas opened-inner-collar, true culm-node, and outer-collar photographic examples are newly archived and have independently inspected arrow targets. No photo proves 1-mm ligule measurement or intact measured sessile/pedicelled pair. Preserve image-specific rights.

beginner_learning_path.title: Silver bluestem — seven real photographs from silver flowering heads to Texas anatomy
beginner_learning_path.intro: Walk from the narrow cottony flowering head and a living clump through an actual rooted voucher, then see Texas photographs of the OPENED INNER blade–sheath collar and the actual CULM NODE. Finish with the awned spikelet and the invasive King Ranch bluestem comparison. Real photographs; the Texas membrane and node lack millimeter calibration, and an intact measured spikelet pair is still missing.
beginner_learning_path.memory_rule: SILVER = numerous SHORT fluffy racemes together in a narrow plume; KR = relatively FEWER LONG finger-like terminal racemes. Confirm with true node/ligule and spikelet evidence before native-grass removal decisions.

steps.title: 1 · Start with a full silvery flowering head
steps.look_for: Notice many crowded SHORT silky flowering branches along a longer, narrow central flowering axis in this real New Mexico plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Head architecture is more dependable than silver-white color; do not count every silky hair as a separate branch.

steps.title: 2 · Find the connected bunch
steps.look_for: Follow the upright flowering culms down to the actual connected BASAL SHOOT CLUMP in this Arizona photo. The roots are underground and are NOT photographed.
steps.why_it_matters: This confirms the grass is a clump-forming perennial; it does not demonstrate that rhizomes are absent. Texas botanical sources disagree on short rhizome presence.

steps.title: 3 · See actual roots attached to the crown
steps.look_for: The real Denver Botanic Gardens herbarium specimen shows a joined basal crown with ACTUAL fibrous roots still physically attached; arrowheads mark only visible plant parts. This specimen was collected in Colorado, not Hays County.
steps.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a photographed perennial base from an aboveground bunch whose roots are hidden. This does not establish whether a local live Texas stand has short rhizomes.

steps.title: 4 · Open the INNER collar to locate the ligule
steps.look_for: Linda Jo Conn's species-identified Milam County, Texas photograph shows the sheath opened to expose a short pale transverse inner lip. No physical 1-mm ruler is present.
steps.why_it_matters: This is where to inspect the real membranous ligule. Do not confuse the leaf sheath with the membrane or claim a measured 1–3 mm length.

steps.title: 5 · Find a true node on the CULM
steps.look_for: In a second photograph of the same Texas specimen, find the actual transverse purple-brown stem band along the pale upright stem. The adjacent green leaf blade is not a node.
steps.why_it_matters: A culm node and the leaf collar are different structures; node color and hairiness vary, and this photograph has no 1-mm ruler.

steps.title: 6 · Check the photographed spikelet and its bent awn
steps.look_for: See the tan elongated spikelet body, fine surrounding pale hairs and an extended DARK bent awn in Liz Makings' original microscope photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Awns are different structures from hairs. The true attached fertile sessile/pedicelled partner pair and upper lemma awn insertion are not visible at organ-level certainty in this photo.

steps.title: 7 · Separate silver from invasive King Ranch
steps.look_for: This is real TEXAS KR bluestem, not silver: trace several much LONGER terminal fingers to their attachment points, then return to photo 1 and its numerous short silvery branches.
steps.why_it_matters: Confusing native silver with introduced KR can lead to unnecessary removal; also check a real cane bluestem true culm node for its long shaggy beard.

beginner_learning_path.safety_note: Do not remove native candidates based on color or one node. The new source-verified Texas collar and node photographs are real and correctly annotated, but not calibrated. An actual 1-mm-measured ligule and intact attached sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair remain genuine research-photo gaps. Nonlocal rooted herbarium specimens do not prove local live rhizomes.
